### Problem: invert a binary tree {#sec-tr-p2-invert}

::: {.p-statement}
Swap the left and right child of every node, and return the root. Values stay where they are.

Constraints: at most $100$ nodes.

Source: [LC 226 · Invert Binary Tree](https://leetcode.com/problems/invert-binary-tree/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The mirror of a tree is the node itself with its two subtrees mirrored and then exchanged. Do the exchange after the recursive calls, or before: both are correct, because the two subtrees do not share nodes. Doing it before is a preorder; doing it after is a postorder. The tree is modified.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Recursion.** Swap, then invert each child (or invert, then swap — the children pointers are what get swapped, so invert the nodes you just attached).
2. **Level order.** Swap the two children of every node the queue pops. No recursion.

**Invariant.** After the call, the subtree is the mirror of what it was, and no node outside it was touched.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Recursion

::: {.form-next}
Exchange the two child pointers, then repeat on each side.
:::


::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def invert(root):
    if root is None:
        return None
    root.left, root.right = invert(root.right), invert(root.left)
    return root
```

##### C++

```cpp
TreeNode* invertTree(TreeNode* root) {
    if (!root) return nullptr;
    TreeNode* left = invertTree(root->left);
    TreeNode* right = invertTree(root->right);
    root->left = right;
    root->right = left;
    return root;
}
```

:::

#### Level order

::: {.form-next}
The same exchange, one node at a time, in level order. Inverting twice restores the original level-order spelling.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get('invert', 'bfs')
    assert str(final) == '[4, 7, 2, 9, 6, 3, 1]'
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def invert_bfs(root):
    if root is None:
        return None
    q = deque([root])
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        u.left, u.right = u.right, u.left
        if u.left:
            q.append(u.left)
        if u.right:
            q.append(u.right)
    return root


src = [4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6, 9]
root = from_level(src)
assert to_level(invert(root)) == [4, 7, 2, 9, 6, 3, 1]
assert to_level(invert(root)) == src
root = from_level(src)
assert to_level(invert_bfs(root)) == [4, 7, 2, 9, 6, 3, 1]
assert invert(None) is None
```

##### C++

```cpp
TreeNode* invertTreeBfs(TreeNode* root) {
    if (!root) return nullptr;
    queue<TreeNode*> q;
    q.push(root);
    while (!q.empty()) {
        auto u = q.front();
        q.pop();
        swap(u->left, u->right);
        if (u->left) q.push(u->left);
        if (u->right) q.push(u->right);
    }
    return root;
}
```

:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
$O(n)$ time. $O(h)$ stack, or $O(\text{width})$ queue. The empty tree returns null.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- One node is already its own mirror.
- `[1,2]` becomes `[1,null,2]`. Dropping the `null` would make the result look like a left child.
- Swapping values instead of child pointers fails as soon as the two sides have different shapes.
- Save both inverted children, then assign them. Writing `left = invert(right)` and then `right = invert(left)` inverts the new left a second time and drops the old left subtree.
- `Node(val, invert(right), invert(left))` returns a mirror and leaves the input tree unchanged. Use it when a later test still needs the original.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- `left = invert(right)` and then `right = invert(left)` inverts the new left a second time and drops the old left. Compute both sides, then assign.
- Swapping the children's values mirrors one level and crashes when a child is missing. Move the subtrees.
- Inverting only one side leaves the other half as it was.
:::

**Variants.** Whether the tree is already its own mirror is [LC 101 · Symmetric Tree](https://leetcode.com/problems/symmetric-tree/){difficulty="Easy"}, and no copy is built. Reversing the values on the odd levels of a perfect tree walks the crossed pairs: [LC 2415 · Reverse Odd Levels of Binary Tree](https://leetcode.com/problems/reverse-odd-levels-of-binary-tree/){difficulty="Medium"}. Sorting the leaves of a perfect tree by swapping children is [CF 1741D · Masha and a Beautiful Tree](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1741/D){rating="1300"}. A new node, instead of an edit, keeps the original tree.
